vignette: Mary, a 77-year-old widow of North American ethnicity, has been struggling with the lasting impact of a man-made disaster that occurred several years ago. As a retired school counselor, she continues to engage in volunteer work at her local community center, but her efforts are often overshadowed by intrusive memories and feelings of intense distress. The traumatic event occurred when Mary was attending a professional development seminar in downtown Toronto. A terrorist attack struck the city, targeting multiple locations, including the conference center where she was present. The explosion shattered windows and filled the room with smoke and debris. Mary recalls feeling a searing pain in her leg as shrapnel embedded itself into her skin. Amidst the chaos, she witnessed people screaming and bleeding, their faces twisted in terror. Since that day, Mary has experienced vivid flashbacks of the event. She often finds herself back in that room, surrounded by the cacophony of alarms and screams. These intrusions can occur at any time but are particularly frequent when she hears loud noises or is in crowded places. The intensity of these recollections leaves her feeling as though she's living through the attack all over again. Mary avoids certain activities and places to mitigate the risk of being triggered. She no longer attends large gatherings, opting instead for smaller, more intimate settings where she feels a greater sense of control. Even simple tasks like watching the news can be overwhelming due to reports about recent disasters or violent incidents. Her social interactions have decreased as she tries to avoid situations that might remind her of the attack. At night, Mary’s sleep is frequently disrupted by nightmares. She dreams of being trapped in a burning building with no way out. Waking up drenched in sweat and gasping for air, she finds it difficult to fall back asleep without feeling a lingering sense of dread. Her sleep deprivation has affected her mood, leaving her more irritable and prone to bursts of anger directed at herself and others. Mary’s hyperarousal is evident in the way she constantly scans her environment for potential threats. When she volunteers at the community center, she can’t help but notice every exit sign, every suspicious individual, and every sound that might indicate danger. This heightened state of vigilance leaves her feeling on edge much of the time. Her relationship with her late husband had been a source of comfort and support. Since his passing two years ago, Mary has felt increasingly isolated in dealing with her symptoms. She often thinks about how he would have helped her navigate these challenges but now finds herself alone, grappling with intense feelings of guilt for not being able to cope better. Mary’s volunteer work at the community center provides a sense of purpose and distraction from her traumatic memories. However, even this outlet is tainted by her PTSD symptoms. She worries about the safety of the children she works with and often imagines worst-case scenarios where an attack could occur again. In conversations, Mary frequently mentions her desire to return to normalcy but acknowledges that it feels increasingly out of reach. Her once vibrant life has been overshadowed by the constant reminders of the disaster, leaving her feeling trapped in a cycle of fear and anxiety. Despite these challenges, Mary remains determined to find moments of peace amidst her struggles. She often reflects on the resilience she witnessed during the attack, both in herself and others, which gives her hope that healing is possible.
